lawyer:
T. H. Khan with A. H. Md. Nurul Huda Khandaker, Advocates ------ For the Petitioners. 
Mahmudul Islam, Assistant Attorney-General  ------ For Respondent No 1.
parties:
Abdur Rashid and another  ------ Petitioners.
Vs.
Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
The Ministry of Industries (Industries Division) Government of Bangladesh by their letter No. IR-XV-23/72/449 Dated 15. 8.73 asked the petitioner No.1" to submit papers in respect of his claim for ownership of the unit in question along with his nationality certificate immediately." This letter has been annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure 'C' The Officer who issued this letter examined ail the documents and the certificate of nationality which were produced in pursuance of this letter before him. But no decision of the government was communicated to the petitioners until the order dated 14. 5. 74 regretting the government's inability to release the properties in question was received by the petitioners. This order has already been quoted above. In controverting the facts stated in the petition, the respondent No. 1 has denied that the petitioner No. 2 was a partner in the Partnership firm named M/S. Moin & Co. It was further stated that since the whereabouts of Moinuddin has not yet been known, and since no presumption can be made that he is dead unless seven years have passed his heirs cannot claim the properties he left. In paragraph 9 of the affidavit-in-opposition the respondent No. 1 has made strenuous efforts to establish that the petitioner No. 2 was not a partner of M/S. Moin & Co. and since in their opinion the petitioner No. 1 had been unable to establish that he was a partner of the said industry he was not entitled to the said premises. 

 3. Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submitted that the properties in question can by no stretch of imagination be viewed as abandoned property even on the facts admitted by the respondent No.1. The facts which have been stated above would show that of the two properties, premises No.150, Nawabpur Road, Dacca is owned by the petitioner No. 2 who has all along been present in Bangladesh beginning from the date when the properties in question were included in the abandoned property list. So far as the other property is concerned i.e. the Soap Industry, which was being carried on in the said premises under the name and style M/S. Moin & Co., even assuming that the petitioner No. 1 is not a partner of the said business and it belonged entirely to deceased Moinuddin, it cannot be said that with his disappearance it became ownerless nor could it be held that it was not being occupied, looked after or supervised by anybody. Admittedly, he left heirs of whom the petitioner No. 2 is the mother. In the presence of petitioner No. 2 and the other heirs of Moinuddin, how can the industry concerned be treated as abandoned property? Whether death can be presumed or not, it is clear that in the absence of the said Moinuddin, his mother, wife and children were there to claim the industry as his heirs as well as look after it. The language as used in Article 2 of the Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal Order, 1972 cannot be construed in the manner suggested by the learned Assistant Attorney-General. His suggestion being that unless the whereabouts of the owner of the properties are known or the presumption of his death can be drawn, the properties must be treated as abandoned property within the meaning of this Article. We cannot take an impossible and unreasonable view of the law laid down in Article 2. The owner may be absent or his whereabouts may not be known but if his family members or heirs, as the case may be, are present in Bangladesh on the relevant date his property cannot be treated as abandoned property. Besides, what interest the government has in taking over the properties in question if it be proved that the heirs or supposed heirs of an absentee owner are present in Bangladesh owing allegiance to the Government of Bangladesh. The impugned, order seems to have been vitiated also for another reason. In a one-line sentence the government has communicated the decision not to release the properties in question without stating any reason whatsoever as to why they decided so. Not only the petitioner produced all the necessary documents in support of their claim to the properties in question and fulfilled the requirements of law as laid down in Article 2 of the President's Order No.1 of 1972 (The Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972, but even the recommendation of the Sub-divisional Officer, Sadar South, Dacca was entirely in favor of releasing the same to the petitioners. We fail to understand why in spite of these circumstances the Government refused to release the properties in question in favor of the petitioners. If on some sort of information the Government had treated the same as an abandoned property, it was their foremost duty to release the same as soon as satisfactory evidence was produced before them that the properties in question could not be treated as abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 due to the circumstances mentioned above. In the absence of ample and proper justification, nothing should come between the citizen and the enjoyment of his properties. No such justification exists in the present case.
